label: What Is a Manifold?
notes: This opening chapter is the runway for the course. It does not give the formal definition yet; instead it builds the mental model of a manifold as a space that may be curved, wrapped, or glued globally while every small neighborhood still looks like ordinary Euclidean space of one fixed dimension.

label: Locally Euclidean
notes: The provisional idea is that an n-manifold looks near each point like n real parameters. The phrase near each point carries the weight. A circle is traced by an angle, but that angle is not a global coordinate because zero and two pi name the same point, so locality is essential.

label: A Gallery of Model Spaces
notes: The gallery compares a circle, a sphere, a torus, and a genus-two surface. Every example carries local coordinates of a fixed dimension, yet only some admit a single global chart. Walking the gallery separates parameterization, local chart, and global model, three ideas that are easy to merge too early.

label: Dimension as Parameter Count
notes: Dimension is the number of independent parameters a local chart records. A circle needs one, a surface needs two, and the three-sphere can be described locally by three. Dimension is intrinsic; it does not depend on the dimension of the ambient space in which we happened to draw the object.

label: Coordinate Charts
notes: A chart is a reversible measurement device. It assigns Euclidean coordinates to points in a neighborhood and reconstructs those points from the coordinates. The goal of the whole subject is to do calculus and topology locally, exactly as we already know how to do them on flat Euclidean space.

label: Stereographic Projection
notes: Stereographic projection makes a chart concrete. Remove one pole, draw a line from it through a point of the sphere, and record where that line meets a flat plane. The map is reversible away from the pole, so a flat two-parameter grid becomes a curved patch covering the sphere minus a single point.

label: Atlases: Why One Chart Fails
notes: No single chart covers the whole sphere, since stereographic projection always misses its pole. A manifold is therefore defined not by one universal coordinate system but by an atlas, a collection of enough compatible local charts whose domains together cover the entire space without gaps.

label: Homeomorphism
notes: Homeomorphism is the chapter's provisional notion of sameness: a continuous bijection with continuous inverse. It ignores metric accidents such as length, angle, and curvature. That is why a cube boundary and a round sphere are the same topological surface even though one has flat faces and sharp edges.

label: Topological Invariants
notes: To prove two spaces are not homeomorphic, pictures fail and invariants succeed. An invariant is data no homeomorphism can change, turning the negative claim into a checkable comparison. If two spaces disagree on an invariant, no homeomorphism between them can exist, which is exactly what we want to certify.

label: Euler Characteristic
notes: Euler characteristic is a coarse invariant for compact surfaces. For orientable surfaces it satisfies chi equals two minus twice the genus, linking it to the number of handles. The sphere scores two, the torus zero, and the genus-two surface minus two, immediately separating these surfaces by an invariant.

label: Classifying Surfaces
notes: A classification pairs a standard list with a checkable signature. Orientable compact surfaces are spheres with g handles; nonorientable ones are spheres with k crosscaps. Knowing orientability and Euler characteristic pins down the surface, demonstrating the pattern of standard family plus invariant formula that the course will later prove rigorously.

label: Roadmap and Takeaways
notes: Chapter one names the recurring pattern the book makes precise. Local Euclidean structure leads to homeomorphism questions, invariants certify non-homeomorphism, and these feed classification. Ahead lie topological spaces, compactness, connectedness, fundamental groups, covering spaces, cell complexes, and the full classification of surfaces, each replacing a node of today's scaffold.
